name: Finger wave hairstyle

card.summary: A 1920s-era sculpted set of S-shaped waves made in wet hair, used to give short hair polished shape and a vintage look.

quick.overview:
Finger waves are smooth S-shaped ripples set into damp hair by pinching and combing it in alternating directions, with a setting lotion to hold the shape. The result is a sleek, sculpted style that frames the face and adds polish to short and medium hair.

The style developed in the 1920s to soften bobbed cuts and was spread by film actresses. It returned in the late 1990s through pop and hip-hop stars and has since appeared on fashion runways.
quick.how: Hairdressers shape wet hair with a comb and fingers using a waving lotion or gel, then secure the waves with clips or tape until dry. Unlike the marcel wave, no heated irons are used. Many people have it set in a salon for events.
quick.risks: A low-risk styling technique. Products with strong hold can dry or stiffen hair, and the shape does not last beyond washing.

lead: Finger waves are a hairstyle in which wet hair is pinched between the fingers and combed into alternating S-shaped waves, held by waving lotion, gel or hairspray, and clipped until dry.[1] The method uses no heated irons, unlike the marcel wave.[1]

The look was developed in the 1920s to soften the bobbed haircuts of the flapper era and was spread by Hollywood stars; the Wikipedia article credits Josephine Baker and Esther Phillips with its early popularity.[1] It is used to give short hair a sculpted, glossy finish.
A late-1990s revival came through pop stars such as Madonna and hip-hop artists such as Missy Elliott, and finger waves appeared on 2016 runways at Marc Jacobs, Prada and other houses.[1]

angle.text: Finger waves add visible shape and shine to short and medium hair for a polished appearance. The set lasts until the hair is washed.

infobox: Comb, waving lotion or gel, clips

paras: The waves are made by combing damp hair and pinching it with the fingers to push it into alternating ridges. A waving lotion, traditionally made with karaya gum and later with gels or hairspray, helps the shape hold, and clips or tape secure it until dry.[1]

Finger waves were developed in the 1920s to soften bobbed cuts, and were most popular in the 1920s and early 1930s in North America and Europe.[1] A 1921 Swarthmore College yearbook photo shows the style, and Paul Compan patented an improved hairdressing comb for making the waves (US patent 1988866).[1] Some claims in the Wikipedia article about earlier history are flagged there as unreliable, so they are not repeated here.
The style returned in the late 1990s, helped by Madonna, Missy Elliott and a shift toward shorter, more natural hair among African-American women, and it appeared on runways in 2016.[1]
